messages.subject: Very slow GLMM
parts:
This is my first time writing up a stan model. I had trouble finding examples of repeated measures analysis. My model compiles, but seems to go very slowly (It has yet to get past 0% warm up). 

This is the model:

data {
  int<lower=1> n; //individuals
  int<lower=1> N; //observations

  int<lower=0> y[N];

  int<lower=0,upper=1> gender[N];
  int<lower=0> age[N];
  int<lower=0> exposure[N];
  int<lower=0,upper=1> treatment[N];
  int<lower=0> time[N];

  int id[N]; 
}
transformed data {
    vector[2] zeros;       
    for (i in 1:2)
      zeros[i] <- 0.0;  
}
parameters {
  real beta0;
  real beta_gender;
  real beta_age;
  real beta_exp;
  real beta_trt;
  real beta_time;
  
  vector[2] gamma[n];
  real<lower=0> sigma0;
  real<lower=0> sigma01;
  real<lower=0> sigma1;
}
transformed parameters {
  real mu[N];
  cov_matrix[2] S;

  S[1,1] <- sigma0;
  S[1,2] <- sigma01;
  S[2,1] <- sigma01;
  S[2,2] <- sigma1;

  for(i in 1:N){
    mu[i] <- exp(beta0 + beta_gender * gender[i]
                       + beta_age * age[i]
                       + beta_exp * exposure[i]
                       + beta_trt * treatment[i]
                       + beta_time * time[i]
                       + gamma[id[i],1] + gamma[id[i],2]*time[i]);
  }
}

model {
  beta0 ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_gender ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_age ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_exp ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_trt ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_time ~ normal(0,100);

  gamma ~ multi_normal(zeros,S);
  
  y ~ poisson(mu);
}

I've also attached the data. Can you guys give me some tips?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very slow GLMM
parts:
Quick tip is to use the noncentered parameterization on gamma; this is on p.63 of the Stan 2.6.2 manual.

Other tip is to use overdispersed Poisson instead of Poisson.  Try the negative binomial distribution.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very slow GLMM
parts:
Your covariance matrix isn't properly constrained. Unlike
in BUGS, we need any valid values of parameters according to
the constraints to have non-zero density.

> parameters {
...

> real<lower=0> sigma0;
> real<lower=0> sigma01;
> real<lower=0> sigma1;
> }
> transformed parameters {
> real mu[N];
> cov_matrix[2] S;
>
> S[1,1] <- sigma0;
> S[1,2] <- sigma01;
> S[2,1] <- sigma01;
> S[2,2] <- sigma1;

You should just declare the cov_matrix as a parameter. Or
better yet, look at the regression chapter in the manual for
a better way to set it up with our recommended priors.

If you insist on doing it this way for some reason, the constraint
is that sigma01 has to be in ( -sigma0 * sigma1, sigma0 * sigma1).
But the name's confusing --- that sigma0 is really a variance, not
a std deviation.

You then want a prior on the covariance matrix.

Also, did you want to do something multilevel or are you
trying to treat time and age and exposure as scalars?

We also don't recommend normal(0,100) priors --- if you really
do expect values in the 100s, you probably want to standardize
predictors instead.

And the parameters gamma probably shouldn't be centered around
zero.

- Bob
